conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope—just for a check-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in today because of a painful swelling in your right groin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. It got really big and then burst on its own. It still hurts, and I’ve been feeling feverish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You went to dialysis earlier today and then came to the ER. They drained the abscess and gave you antibiotics. You’re on vancomycin for now to cover any serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had abscesses here before. Last time, I got really sick—sepsis from a gallbladder infection. I’m worried it could happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. We’re watching you closely. Your vitals are stable, and your blood work doesn’t show signs of sepsis. We’ve started you on IV antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been nauseous and not eating much. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related. Sometimes infections affect your appetite. We’ll keep an eye on it. We gave you something for nausea earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. And my blood pressure—it’s been low lately after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed that. It tends to dip after dialysis, but it comes back up quickly. We’re using a Doppler to check your BP more accurately because of your size.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had trouble with that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria growing. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection in the blood? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That means the antibiotics are likely doing their job, and you’re not in sepsis. We’ll keep you on vancomycin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the abscess? Is it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgical team checked it—they don’t think it’s spreading. No signs of a deeper infection like Fournier’s gangrene.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I was really scared of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a CT scan today to make sure the infection isn’t tracking deeper into your pelvis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s just a scan with contrast. You’ll lie still for about 20 minutes. We need to rule out any hidden pockets of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. Good news—no abscess or fluid collection in your pelvis. The infection seems contained to the surface.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I heard something about a possible blood clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT showed a possible issue in your right groin vein, so we ordered an ultrasound to check for a blood clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had clots before. I’m on warfarin already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re being cautious. Your INR was therapeutic, but we’ll confirm with the ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. No DVT in the major veins of your right leg. The calf veins weren’t fully seen, but we don’t think there’s a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I can keep taking my warfarin the same way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your current dose. Antibiotics can affect warfarin, so we’ll monitor your INR before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look good. White count is normal, and you’ve stayed afebrile since admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The abscess is improving, and you’re responding well to treatment. We’ll keep the packing in for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you in a day or two. You’ll finish a week of antibiotics through dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We changed one of your medications—stopped Renvela and started sevelamer carbonate. It’s similar but better for your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’m still taking my other pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your other meds continue—insulin, amiodarone, simvastatin, paroxetine. We added a daily vitamin—Nephrocaps—for kidney patients.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get it during dialysis for one more week. After that, no more IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the packing? How long do I need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Every other day until the wound heals. A nurse at your facility will do it. Call if it starts draining more or gets red and hot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Should I watch my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds—it could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. My heart and kidneys don’t like extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing well—no signs of heart failure or breathing trouble. Your oxygen levels are stable on 2 liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is therapeutic, and your labs are stable. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: To the extended care facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They’ll continue your wound care, dialysis, and antibiotics. Make sure they get your updated med list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me. I was really worried this would turn bad again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Just keep up with the packing, take your meds, and call if you feel feverish or unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll try to use my CPAP more, even though I don’t like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would help your oxygen and sleep. But we know it’s tough. Just do your best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. You completed your dialysis session fine, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel okay. A bit tired, but no pain or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Keep resting, stay on your meds, and keep the wound clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad I’m not back in the ICU like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This time, we caught it early and treated it quickly. That made all the difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m grateful. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. Have a safe trip to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your groin wound started bleeding during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it just started oozing. I was scared. My blood pressure dropped, they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your hematocrit dropped from 36 to 30, and your INR was high at 3.0. We stopped the bleeding with medication and packing. But we need to find out why this keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infection again? I just had that abscess drained last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. A scan showed a possible pseudoaneurysm near your wound, but a later CT confirmed something more serious—an arteriovenous fistula in your groin. That means an artery and vein are connected abnormally, which can cause bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Can that be fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it will require surgery. We’ll need to go in and close off those abnormal connections. Given your history—ESRD, diabetes, clotting issues—it’s high risk, but necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on warfarin. Isn’t that making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It contributes. Your INR was 3.0, which is high. We’ve held your warfarin for now. We’ll restart it later when it’s safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your regular schedule. We’ll coordinate it around your care. For now, you’re admitted for monitoring and prep for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. The CT confirmed the AV fistula comes from the profunda and common femoral arteries. We’ve scheduled surgery for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I lose a lot of blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There is risk, yes. These vessels are large. We’re preparing for possible transfusion. But the team is experienced, and we’ll do everything to keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in recovery. The surgery went well. We took down the fistulas. But you did lose about 4.5 liters of blood. You received fluids, red cells, and FFP. You’re in the ICU for close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So much blood… am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable now. Hemodynamically okay. We’re watching your kidney function and heart closely. You’ll move to the floor tomorrow if all stays well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re off the ventilator and moving to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My wound still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will for a while. We’re keeping it clean and watching for infection. You’re still on antibiotics from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk. On day 6 after surgery, you developed redness and drainage at the incision site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We opened and packed the wound. The culture grew two bacteria: Klebsiella and Proteus. They’re resistant to many antibiotics, but sensitive to meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re changing my antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching from vancomycin, cipro, and flagyl to IV meropenem. It covers both organisms effectively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need it long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about two weeks. We’ll give it through a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line today for your antibiotics. You have poor vein access, so we’ll use ultrasound and X-ray guidance in your right arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local anesthesia. It’s a quick procedure. The line will stay in for your antibiotics and then be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully yesterday. Your wound is being debrided daily. We’re seeing granulation tissue, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s granulation tissue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s new tissue that forms during healing. Pink and bumpy. It means your wound is starting to close from the inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need the infection under control and the wound stable. You’ll likely go to extended care for wound management and IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a wound VAC today. It’s a vacuum device that helps pull fluid out and encourages healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel a pulling sensation, but it’s usually well tolerated. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is improving. Less drainage, more granulation. The VAC is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugars? They’ve been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stress and steroids can raise them. We’ve adjusted your insulin. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest wound culture confirmed Klebsiella and Proteus. Both are sensitive to meropenem, so we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can be, especially with your health conditions. But meropenem is strong and effective. We’re confident it will clear the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. The wound no longer needs debridement. We’ll keep the VAC a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start walking more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with assistance. We’ll get physical therapy to help you build strength. But avoid straining the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis went well yesterday. Your labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To extended care. You’ll continue the VAC, get IV meropenem through the PICC, and have wound checks daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing discharge. You’ll go with the VAC, PICC line, and a 14-day course of meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are resuming: simvastatin, pantoprazole, sevelamer, and warfarin at a lower dose. Paroxetine is cut in half. We’re adding cinacalcet for your calcium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your surgeon in two weeks. The wound team will manage the VAC and PICC. Call us if you develop fever, increased redness, or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—the CT also showed fibroids and a small spot in your labia. It could be a hematoma. Your gynecologist will evaluate it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s small. We’ll follow up after you’ve healed from this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Hemodynamically stable, eating well, wound improving. We’re scheduling discharge for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so scared when I started bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But you’ve been strong. This was complex, but we’ve addressed the fistula and infection. Now it’s about healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last check. Your wound is ready for transfer. Remember: keep the VAC on, watch for fever, and don’t skip dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. You’re being discharged to extended care with wound VAC and PICC for antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks to you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.
