conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You were admitted today because of your right heel wound that’s been getting worse. We’re going to take a close look and make sure we treat it properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. It’s been really painful and dry, and I noticed it’s turning black around the edges.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s called dry gangrene, and it means the tissue is dying due to poor blood flow. We’re concerned about infection and how well it can heal with your circulation issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had circulation problems before. Does this mean I might lose my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not there yet. Right now, we’re focusing on treating the infection and seeing how bad the blood flow is. We’ve ordered a CT scan with contrast to check your arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’m on dialysis too—will that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate your dialysis as usual. In fact, you’re scheduled tomorrow. We’ll give your antibiotics during dialysis to make sure they work well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also on Coumadin. Is that safe with the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping it because of your history of blood clots. We’ll monitor your levels closely so you don’t bleed, but also don’t clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan came back. There’s severe hardening and narrowing in your leg arteries—especially behind the knee and down to the foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there any blood getting through at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The front artery—the anterior tibial—is still open and supplying blood to your foot. But the others are heavily calcified and blocked. That’s why healing is so hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about that fistula in my groin? I had that fixed before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the scan shows the AV fistula is still there—between the artery and vein in your right groin. It’s not the main issue now, but we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So what’s next for the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started IV antibiotics—vancomycin and cipro—to cover possible infection. Podiatry will come to clean the wound later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they cut away the dead part?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s called debridement. They’ll remove the dead tissue to help prevent infection from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The podiatry team debrided your heel yesterday. The wound looks cleaner, but it’s still not healing due to poor circulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what are my options now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did an ultrasound today to confirm the CT findings. The blood flow is very poor below your knee. Given how severe the blockages are, the vascular team feels a bypass isn’t possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… does that mean amputation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, yes. A below-knee amputation is likely the only long-term solution to prevent infection and relieve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not ready for that yet. Can I try to manage it without surgery for now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We respect your decision. We’ll continue antibiotics, wound care, and close monitoring. But you need to know the risks—like infection spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just need more time to think about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria in the bloodstream. That’s good news. It means the infection hasn’t spread systemically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my dialysis meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nephrology team reviewed your labs. Your PTH was elevated, so they stopped sevelamer and calcitrol and started high-dose vitamin D once a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help my bones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps regulate calcium and phosphorus, which is important for bone health, especially with kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. We’ll switch your antibiotics from IV to an oral one—Bactrim—for three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my allergies? I’m allergic to penicillin and ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bactrim is unrelated to those. But we’ll watch you closely, especially since you’re also on warfarin. There can be interactions, so we’ve adjusted the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Where will I go after here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to an extended care facility. They can help with wound care, dialysis coordination, and monitoring your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need close follow-up with vascular surgery. If the wound starts draining, you develop a fever, or pain worsens, you should come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I might need the amputation later. I’ll think about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely okay. We’ll support whatever decision you make, but we want you to stay safe and avoid serious complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just reviewing your discharge meds. You’ll take warfarin daily, Bactrim twice a day for three weeks, and the weekly vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin and pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same insulin doses—2 units at breakfast and bedtime, plus sliding scale if needed. For pain, you can take Dilaudid or Tylenol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my cholesterol and heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue simvastatin, amiodarone, and pantoprazole. We kept them all since they’re important for your heart, lungs, and reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have depression. Is Paxil still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing paroxetine. Mental health is just as important, especially during tough decisions like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Remember to weigh yourself daily and call your doctor if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep my appointments with vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Take care, and don’t hesitate to come back if anything changes with your wound or how you feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your wound is dry gangrene now, but if it becomes wet, smelly, or starts draining, that’s an emergency. Come in right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll watch it every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, since you’re on oxygen at home, make sure your tubing isn’t pressing on the wound or limiting movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. I don’t want to make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well this week. We’ll send all your records to the extended care facility and your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I feel more prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here to support you, no matter what you decide about surgery in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you to the extended care facility in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these printed instructions with you. Call us if you have any questions after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital because you weren’t feeling well and were confused. We found a serious infection in your right foot. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I remember being in rehab. Then they said I wasn’t eating. I don’t remember much after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. Your blood pressure was low and your white blood cell count was very high, which means your body is fighting a severe infection. The ulcer on your heel is infected and has gangrene.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gangrene? Like… dead tissue? I had that before. They said I might need an amputation, but I didn’t want it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the infection has spread. Because of poor blood flow from your vascular disease, antibiotics alone won’t clear it. Vascular surgery has reviewed your case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… you’re saying I need to lose my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They recommend a below-knee amputation to stop the infection from spreading. It’s the safest option right now. We’ll manage your pain and support you through recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. I don’t want to lose more of my leg. But if it’s the only way… okay. Do what you have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get you prepped for surgery tomorrow. We’ve started IV antibiotics—vancomycin, flagyl, and aztreonam—to control the infection until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re in recovery after your below-knee amputation. The surgery went well. The team removed the infected part of your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts… but I can’t feel my foot. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected. You’ll have some phantom sensations. We’re giving IV hydromorphone for pain and will switch to oral medicine soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound culture showed Proteus mirabilis and Klebsiella pneumoniae—both resistant to several antibiotics. Infectious disease recommends switching to IV imipenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger? Will it work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, imipenem covers these bacteria well. We’ll continue it for now and monitor your response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your leg. There’s no abscess or bone infection, which is good. But there’s still swelling and poor healing due to poor blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So am I healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is improving, but the blood flow is still very poor. Vascular surgery is concerned the wound may not heal with just a below-knee amputation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk. The surgical site isn’t getting enough blood. They’re recommending an above-knee amputation to ensure healing and prevent reinfection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another one? I just had surgery! I don’t know if I can do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s a lot. But leaving the poorly perfused tissue increases the risk of the infection coming back, which could be life-threatening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it’s the only way to survive… then yes. Do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before your next surgery, we need to move your dialysis access from your groin to your neck. It’s safer and has lower infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? I’m so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But it’s important. Because you’re on warfarin, we’ll stop it and use a heparin drip temporarily to prevent clots during the switch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The neck line was placed successfully in your external jugular vein. You’ll start dialysis through it tomorrow. We’ve restarted the heparin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, dialysis will work the same. But this access is more stable and easier to care for long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis went well last night. Your labs are improving—white count is down to 18. The imipenem is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When’s the next surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for tomorrow. We’ll do the above-knee amputation. Your pain will be managed closely after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from surgery. The above-knee amputation was completed. The team removed the remaining non-viable tissue. You’re in the recovery phase now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s really gone… I can’t believe it. I feel numb.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a big adjustment. We’ve switched your pain meds to oral oxycodone. Physical therapy will start working with you soon to help you adapt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family visited yesterday and mentioned you were upset. Is everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just… I don’t know how I’ll live like this. No leg, always on dialysis. I feel like I’m falling apart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ve involved social work. They can help you process this and connect you with counseling after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be depressed. I’m just… sad. And tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay to feel that way. You’re on paroxetine, which we’ll continue. Talking to someone can really help. Would you like to meet with the counselor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The counselor spoke with you and said you felt a bit better. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She helped. I still have bad days, but I know I’m not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low when we stopped warfarin for surgery. We’re using a heparin drip to protect you from clots until your INR comes back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on blood thinners for years. Is it safe to be off them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not completely, which is why we’re using heparin. Once your INR is above 2.0, we can stop the drip and restart your warfarin at 2 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is now 9.8—back to normal. The infection is cleared. We’ll finish the imipenem course and stop antibiotics soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not home yet. You’ll go to an extended care facility. You need physical therapy and the heparin drip until your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is healing well. No signs of infection. Vascular surgery will see you in two weeks after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m learning to use the wheelchair. It’s hard, but I’m doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 1.7. Still low. You’ll keep the heparin drip at the facility until it reaches 2.0 or higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then I can stop the IV medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Once your INR is therapeutic, they’ll stop the heparin and you’ll stay on warfarin 2 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge tomorrow. You’ll go to extended care for rehab and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but ready. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most stay the same. Warfarin is now 2 mg daily. You’ll get vitamin D weekly. Pain meds are oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue three times a week through your neck line. The facility will coordinate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we removed the old dialysis line from your groin. The site is healing well. Your new neck line is working perfectly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. That one always worried me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. You’ve made it through a tough journey.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m scared, but I know what to expect now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have support. Keep taking your meds, attend PT, and follow up with vascular surgery in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And… thank you for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard work. We’re proud of you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. I understand you came in because of drainage and discomfort from your right leg amputation site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been oozing this smelly fluid for a few days now. I was worried it might be infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we brought you in. We examined your stump and saw some wound separation and signs of infection. We’ll start antibiotics and do a debridement to clean it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Debridement? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we’ll remove any dead or infected tissue from the wound so healthy tissue can grow. It’s done at the bedside, not in the operating room, and we’ll give you pain medicine first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just don’t want another big surgery. I’m still recovering from the above-knee amputation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This isn’t another major surgery. It’s a necessary step to help your wound heal. We’ll also continue the IV antibiotics you were on—imipenem—because we’ve seen Proteus and Klebsiella before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Those bacteria again? They caused so much trouble last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re being careful. Infectious disease is helping us manage this. We’ll get a deeper culture today to see exactly what’s growing now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis? I’m supposed to go tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on your regular dialysis schedule. You’re due tomorrow at noon—we’ve already arranged it. We’ll monitor your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My blood pressure and sugar can get tricky on dialysis days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on both. You’re on insulin and your home meds will continue unless we adjust them. We’ve also restarted your Coumadin for blood clots, with heparin as backup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I stopped Coumadin, I got clots in my neck veins. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly why we’re continuing it. You’re at high risk, so we’re being very cautious with your anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray last night was stable—some atelectasis in the lower lung, but no pneumonia. Your heart is enlarged, which we knew, but no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I sometimes feel short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Your heart doesn’t pump as efficiently, and your sleep apnea doesn’t help. We have you on oxygen and will encourage breathing exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I should use my CPAP, but it’s uncomfortable. Maybe I’ll try harder when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would help a lot. For now, we’re focused on your wound. The culture from yesterday showed Proteus mirabilis again, which is resistant to many antibiotics, but sensitive to imipenem—so we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the other bacteria? You mentioned Klebsiella before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This culture also grew Enterococcus. It’s not as sensitive to vancomycin, but it is to daptomycin. We’re adding that antibiotic before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More IV meds? How long will I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both antibiotics for several weeks. You’ll go to extended care after discharge, where nurses will give the IVs. Then follow-up with infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess that makes sense. I just want this wound to finally heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do too. The debridement yesterday helped expose healthy tissue. We’ll do another one today if needed and then start a vacuum dressing to help it close.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on dialysis yesterday. Your potassium and fluid levels are stable. But your sodium is a bit low—132—so we’re asking you to limit fluids to 1.5 liters a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only 1.5 liters? That’s not much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard, but too much water can worsen swelling and lower sodium further. We’ll track your intake closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. How’s the wound looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Better. After the second debridement, we saw good granulation tissue—pink and healthy. We’ve started twice-daily moist-to-dry dressings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more debridements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The next step is a vacuum-assisted closure device, or ‘vac,’ which helps pull the wound together. We’ll wait until the tissue is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your latest labs show your white count is down, and CRP is improving. That means the infection is responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been feeling better, less tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is under control too. You’re using Dilaudid only once or twice a day, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain is manageable now. When do you think I can go to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If things keep improving, we’re looking at discharge in a few days. You’ll go to extended care for wound care and physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to place the vacuum dressing tomorrow. The wound looks ready—healthy tissue, no dead areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you pain medicine first. Most patients say it’s uncomfortable but not painful. It really helps healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it. I just want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The vac is in place and working well. You tolerated it fine. We’ll change it every few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels tight, but not bad. My leg feels cleaner somehow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. The infection markers are continuing to improve. We’ll keep both antibiotics going at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is back to 135—great job on fluid restriction. We’re going to write that order out so your rehab team knows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been measuring my water. It’s tough, but I see it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning discharge for tomorrow. You’ll go to Willow Creek Rehab Center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of them. They have good physical therapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and they’re experienced with wound care and dialysis patients. You’ll continue dialysis three times a week there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge prep. You’ll take daptomycin IV every other day and imipenem twice daily. A nurse will give them at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin and other pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds continue—amiodarone, insulin, Coumadin, pantoprazole, Paxil. We’ve updated the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I can keep taking Paxil. After my last amputation, I was really down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of that and glad you’re doing better emotionally. Keep talking to your counselor at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about warning signs? When should I call?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever over 101, increased redness, pus, or bleeding from the wound. Also, if you feel short of breath or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vac? Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No showering until the vac is removed. The rehab team will manage it. No soaking the leg in water for four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’re afebrile, eating well, and your wound looks stable. We’re confident you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous but ready. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up the good work at rehab. Follow up with vascular surgery and infectious disease. You’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—when can I start trying to walk with a prosthesis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. First, the wound must fully heal. Vascular surgery will assess you in a few weeks. It’s a process, but you’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be patient. I just want to be independent again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will be. One step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. Remember: elevate your leg, keep it clean, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch with your rehab team. You’ve done great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep working hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. See you soon in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re all rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks to you and the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard part. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had fevers, chills, and a cough. My dialysis nurse said my catheter site looked infected. I’ve also been nauseous and not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your vitals show a fever and your white blood cell count is high, which suggests an infection. We’ve started you on vancomycin for the catheter infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious? I’ve had infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this is serious—severe sepsis. The infection is in your bloodstream from the catheter. We’ll remove the line and get you on the right antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to remove your right neck catheter today. It’s infected and needs to come out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll place a temporary line in your left groin later so you can continue dialysis safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter was successfully removed. Cultures confirmed MRSA, so we’re continuing vancomycin. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA? I’ve heard that’s tough to treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but your strain is sensitive to vancomycin, which is effective. We’ll keep you on it for several weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray after the procedure looks good—no pneumonia or pneumothorax. Lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing. Could it be the flu?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested for flu—both A and B were negative. Your cough is likely from mild fluid in the lungs, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned belly pain. We did a CT scan—no blockage or serious issue. It’s likely constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts a lot. What can we do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a tap water enema. It should help. We’ll also start daily polyethylene glycol to prevent it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have new back pain. Could the infection have spread?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a concern with MRSA bacteremia. We’ll check your ESR and CRP, and possibly do an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your inflammatory markers are high, but your exam doesn’t show spine tenderness. We’ll do an echocardiogram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The echo was suboptimal, but no vegetations seen. Given your history, we’ll do a TEE under anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’ve had trouble with sedation before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, anesthesia will monitor you closely. It’s important to rule out endocarditis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The TEE is done. No vegetations found. That’s excellent news—no heart infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a temporary femoral line this morning. Your right jugular vein is blocked, so we can’t reuse it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-ray confirms the temporary line is in good position. We’re planning a tunneled version soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back pain is getting better. Did the antibiotics help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely so. With no signs of abscess or osteomyelitis, and your markers improving, it’s resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding warfarin because of the procedures. You’re on heparin now to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on warfarin for DVTs. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safe short-term with heparin. We’ll restart warfarin later and monitor your INR closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—8.2 now, from 17.3. That means the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You need the tunneled catheter and stable INR before discharge. Probably another week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m constipated again. Can I have the enema?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give it now. We’ve added daily polyethylene glycol to help prevent this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to reopen your right jugular vein today, but it’s too blocked. We’ll proceed with the left femoral tunneled line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your tunneled catheter is in place and working. It’s more secure for long-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to go to rehab soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re waiting for your INR to stabilize on warfarin and to confirm blood cultures are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now therapeutic at 2.5. That’s one step closer to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My leg hurts near the catheter. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with ultrasound—no hematoma or abscess. There’s some swelling, but it’s healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All recent blood cultures are negative. That means the bacteremia is clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How long will I need IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue vancomycin through dialysis for about six weeks, managed at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another ultrasound shows no hematoma. The catheter site is stable, with slight oozing—normal for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired of being here. What’s left?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check of labs and vitals. If all looks good, we’ll plan discharge in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your WBC is normal, CRP is down. You’re improving steadily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled your transfer to extended care. They’ll manage dialysis and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—weekly blood tests at dialysis, including vancomycin levels and INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’ll take warfarin daily and watch for bleeding or infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Inspect it daily. Redness, swelling, or pus means call your provider right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last check—vitals are stable, labs acceptable. You’re cleared for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to start recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Rehab will support your healing. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my diabetes. My sugars were high when I ate food from home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed. Keep using the sliding scale insulin and stick to the low-potassium, low-fluid diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here to help. Rehab will continue your care seamlessly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Remember your follow-up with infectious disease in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have it written down. I’ll keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and we’ll see you if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is proud of your progress. Keep fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. You came in with nausea and feeling unwell—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this nausea for about a week. I’m not throwing up, but I just feel off. I also have a dry cough and last night I had bad night sweats.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, belly pain, or changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No belly pain. I did have a bowel movement yesterday after taking milk of magnesia, but before that I can’t remember when. I’ve been constipated for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your labs and your potassium was high earlier, but it’s better now. Your kidney function is stable with dialysis. We also saw a shadow on your chest X-ray, so we started antibiotics just in case it’s pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know. But I feel hungry now—does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. You’re not in distress, and your breathing is fine. We’ll keep monitoring. We also noticed a rash on your lower back—does that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s sore and itchy. I’ve had it for a while, but it hasn’t healed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care looked at it and thinks it’s a fungal rash with a small skin crack. We’re going to start an antifungal cream and make sure you’re not sitting on it too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your infection markers are normal, and the chest X-ray shadow is likely old. We’re stopping the antibiotics since it doesn’t look like pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the nausea isn’t from an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so. Your gallbladder ultrasound didn’t show any active issues, and your liver tests are stable. Given your history of reflux and obesity, we think it might be related to stomach acid. We’ve started you on omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—I’ve had heartburn before. But what about the mass in my breast? I’m worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. The mass needs follow-up with breast surgery. It could be serious, so please make that appointment as soon as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving, and you’re feeling better. We’re going to discharge you to extended care today where you can continue dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I keep taking the new medicine for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take omeprazole daily. Also keep using the antifungal cream for your rash, and don’t forget to follow up with dermatology. And please see the breast surgeon about the mass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep an eye on your weight—call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. Otherwise, you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’ll go to extended care today, and all your medications are listed, including insulin, warfarin, and the new omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking magnesium citrate for constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once a week, or more if needed. The polyethylene glycol and senna are also there to help. Stay on top of it—constipation can make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to follow up on everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re alert, eating, and your vitals are stable. We’re confident you’ll do well with the right follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than yesterday. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The transport team will take you to extended care shortly. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. You’ve been admitted today because of the breast masses we’ve been monitoring. We’re here to get you ready for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thank you. I’ve been nervous about this. I still can’t feel the lumps myself, but I know they’ve grown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very common. Many women don’t feel breast masses even when they’re visible on imaging. The mammogram showed two areas that increased in size—from 9mm and 5mm to 14mm and 8mm—so we want to remove them to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my cousin had breast cancer, so I’m worried it might be the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Family history does increase risk, but we won’t know for sure until after the surgery and pathology. Right now, we’re treating this as suspicious, which is why we’re moving forward with the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also take Coumadin for blood clots. I read that might be a problem with surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because you’re on long-term anticoagulation for deep vein thrombosis, we need to temporarily stop Coumadin and switch to a heparin drip. That’s called a ‘heparin bridge.’ It keeps your blood thin but can be reversed quickly before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. So I’m on heparin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we started the heparin drip this afternoon. We’re monitoring your PTT to make sure it’s in the right range—between 60 and 80. Your INR was 2.6 earlier, which is a bit high for surgery, so holding Coumadin was the right move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about dialysis? I usually go every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You received dialysis today before admission, and you’re scheduled again for Thursday. We’ll keep to your usual schedule. We’re also watching your fluid and potassium closely—so you’re on a 1.5-liter fluid limit and low-potassium diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’m used to it. But will I be able to breathe okay during surgery? I have sleep apnea and use oxygen at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You’ll continue your home oxygen during your stay. The anesthesia team knows about your sleep apnea and will monitor you closely. You’ll also be on supplemental oxygen after surgery until we’re sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a little better knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today is the day for your wire localization. You’ll go to radiology first, where they’ll place two small wires to mark the exact spots of the masses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll use local anesthesia, so you’ll be awake but numb in the area. It might feel like pressure, but not sharp pain. Once the wires are in, you’ll go straight to surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the surgery—what exactly will they do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a wire-localized partial mastectomy. The surgeon will remove the tissue around each wire, including the masses, and also do a ‘global re-excision’ to make sure the margins are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Margins clear? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means no cancer cells at the edge of the removed tissue. That’s a good sign—shows we got it all. If not, we might need more surgery later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it’s clear. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you did great. The surgery is over. You’re in recovery now. The procedure went smoothly, and you tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. Was everything removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both masses were successfully removed. The specimen x-ray confirmed the lesions were taken out with the wires. You’ll have a drain in place for a few days to prevent fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the heparin? Is that stopped now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped the heparin about 10 hours before surgery and restarted it 10 hours after. It’s running again now. We’ll keep it going until your INR is back in the therapeutic range on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m on a lot of meds—will they all go back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your home medications adjusted for dialysis. Omeprazole, amiodarone, paroxetine, insulin—all are being given as usual. We’re watching your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit sore, but okay. The drain is uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on the output. Once it drops below 30cc per day, we can remove it. Any fever, chills, or redness around the site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show mild anemia—hemoglobin is 8.8, which is expected with your kidney disease. We’re not giving a transfusion unless it drops further. You’re also on nephrocaps and Sensipar for bone and mineral balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take those at home. And I have that fungal rash on my sacrum from the last stay—any chance it came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse checked this morning—no rash now. We’re keeping the area clean and dry. You’re on contact isolation because of past MRSA and VRE, but you’re not infected now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we got an update from pathology. The final report shows multifocal invasive ductal carcinoma—two tumors, 0.6cm and 1.2cm. But the margins are clear. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Invasive? That sounds serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the cancer started in the milk ducts and spread a small amount into surrounding tissue. But because it’s small and the margins are clear, surgery may be all you need. Oncology will review and let us know if you need chemo or radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So I might not need more treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly not. It depends on hormone receptor status and other markers, which are still pending. But right now, we’re optimistic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your drain output is down to 25cc today. We’ll remove it tomorrow if it stays low. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I only took acetaminophen once last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re also doing well on the diabetic, low-sodium diet. Blood pressure and glucose are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have dialysis today, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re scheduled for hemodialysis this afternoon. We’ll make sure the access site is clean and the team knows about your recent surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The drain is out, and the incision looks great—no signs of infection. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll need someone to help you at home for a few days. No lifting more than 5 pounds for at least two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sister can stay with me. What about my Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on Coumadin at 5mg daily. Your INR was 2.6 this morning—perfect. Keep taking it at the same time every day, and avoid foods high in vitamin K.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like spinach and kale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll send you home with a list of foods to limit. Also, continue your insulin, omeprazole, and constipation meds—senna and MiraLAX—as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. Dialysis went well yesterday. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Do I need to see anyone after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll follow up with your surgeon in one week. Oncology will contact you about next steps. Also, keep your regular appointments with nephrology, primary care, and dermatology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis continues as usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to your normal schedule. Call your doctor if you have fever, increased pain, redness, or drainage from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.
